Accrual accounting records income and expenses when they happen, not when money moves. So if you bill a customer in June but they pay in July, the sale shows up in June. The same goes for bills: an expense is recorded when you incur it, even if you pay later. Cash-basis accounting does the opposite — you only record income when you receive cash and expenses when you actually pay them.

Accrual gives a clearer picture of ongoing profitability and matches revenues with the costs to earn them, which helps with planning and comparing periods. Cash basis is simpler and can make short-term cash flow easier to see, so small or very cash-focused businesses sometimes use it. Larger companies and formal financial reporting usually use accrual accounting because it shows business performance more accurately.
